design_detail: Pooled descriptive analysis of flashback phenomena in all six double-blind, placebo-controlled, randomized crossover trials of LSD or psilocybin in healthy volunteers run by one research group in Basel up to April 2021. Flashbacks were recorded as adverse events at sessions and asked about once at an end-of-study visit; participants who reported them were followed up by email in May 2021. Frequencies are descriptive; there is no comparison with a no-drug condition.
can_establish: How many healthy, screened trial participants reported flashback-like experiences after LSD or psilocybin when asked at the end of a controlled study, what those experiences were like (sense, length, frequency, feeling, timing) and whether any met DSM-5 criteria for hallucinogen persisting perception disorder (HPPD).
cannot_establish: Whether the drug caused the reported experiences (no estimate of how often similar experiences occur without a drug; an earlier psilocybin analysis found similar rates before and after dosing); frequencies in people who use LSD or psilocybin outside research, with psychiatric histories, frequent use or other drugs; flashbacks starting after the end-of-study visit in people who reported none (only those with flashbacks were followed up); and the true rate of HPPD (a zero count in 142 people is compatible with a rate up to about 2%).

sample.recruitment: All participants of the six LSD or psilocybin trials conducted by the Basel group as of April 2021 (NCT01878942, NCT02308969, NCT03019822, NCT03321136, NCT03604744, NCT03912974); four enrolled participants dropped out before receiving a study drug (Methods › Studies included in analysis; Results › Subject characteristics).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Ages 25 to 65 (25 to 50 in one trial), German-speaking, willing to avoid illicit drugs during the study. Excluded: personal or first-degree family history of seizures or of psychotic or major psychiatric disorder, cardiac or neurological disorders, more than ten prior illicit drug uses (cannabis excepted) or any illicit use in the previous two months, pregnancy or nursing, interfering medicines.
sample.demographics: Mean age 31.7 (SD 9.0); 74 women and 68 men; previous hallucinogen use in 30.3% (mean 2.2 occasions), MDMA in 40.1%, other stimulants in 34.5%, cannabis in 78.9% (Results › Subject characteristics; Table 1).
sample.attrition: Follow-up was sought only from the 13 who reported flashbacks: one could not be reached and another gave incomplete information. Whether all participants who dropped out after a session (at least two of the 13) had a full end-of-study visit is not stated.
sample.selection_effects: Healthy volunteers with little previous drug experience and no psychiatric history, likely with positive attitudes towards psychedelics, as the authors note; people who had had bad after-effects before may have been less likely to enrol.

exposure.measurement: Randomized administration of LSD, psilocybin or comparators under double-blind, placebo-controlled conditions in six crossover trials; every participant also had placebo sessions.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: LSD 0.025 to 0.2 mg by mouth (capsules, or a solution in ethanol), 213 administrations, 1 to 5 per person; psilocybin 15 to 30 mg by mouth (capsules of 5 mg), 103 administrations, 1 or 2 per person. The two single-dose LSD trials used 0.1 mg (n = 24 in Table 1) and 0.2 mg (n = 16 in Table 1); one trial compared LSD 0.1 mg with d-amphetamine 40 mg and MDMA 125 mg; one compared LSD 0.025 to 0.2 mg and LSD with ketanserin; one gave psilocybin 25 mg after pretreatment with escitalopram (20 mg in Table 1; the person in Table 2 had two 10 mg doses) or placebo; one compared LSD 0.1 and 0.2 mg with psilocybin 15 and 30 mg. Flashbacks counted if more than 24 hours after a dose. End-of-study visit a mean of 39.8 days (SD 37.2, range 2 to 193) after the last session; follow-up a mean of 31.2 months (SD 28.6, range 3.3 to 86.8) after that visit.
exposure.polysubstance: Illicit drugs prohibited during the trials; alcohol and caffeine avoided the evening before and on session days. Three of the 13 people with flashbacks had also received a non-hallucinogenic study drug (escitalopram, d-amphetamine or MDMA).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Not applicable: the outcome is recurrence of drug-like experiences after the acute effects had ended.

comparison.controls: None for the flashback outcome. Placebo sessions existed within each crossover trial, but flashback reports could not be attributed to a placebo condition and no no-drug rate is given.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Tendency to unusual perceptual experiences, migraine, tinnitus and anxiety, proposed risk factors for HPPD, were not measured.

outcomes.instruments: Open questions about any flashback phenomena at each session and at the end-of-study visit, with description of quality, quantity, impairment and timing; email follow-up asking about further flashbacks, frequency, impairment and triggers; ICD-10 (F16.7) definition of flashbacks and DSM-5 criteria for HPPD applied by the authors.
outcomes.validity_norms: No validated questionnaire; the authors note that heightened awareness of ordinary perceptual experiences may explain some reports.
outcomes.operationalization: Flashback: recurrence of drug-like experiences after the acute effects had ended (the study's time threshold is recorded in the exposure field). HPPD: persisting flashback phenomena with clinically significant distress or impairment (DSM-5).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: Not applicable; by the end-of-study visit participants were usually unblinded to the substances received across the trial.

analysis.effect_sizes: Descriptive percentages without confidence intervals: 13 of 142 (9.2%) reported flashback phenomena; 7 of 90 after LSD only (7.8%), 2 of 24 after psilocybin only (8.3%), 4 of 28 after both (14.3%); 2 of 142 (1.4%) distressing; 0 of 142 met DSM-5 criteria for HPPD. Simulated probability of observing no case of HPPD in 142 people: 24.0% for a true incidence of 1%, 5.7% for 2%, 1.3% for 3%, 0.3% for 4%, 0.1% for 5%. Editors' calculation: with zero events in 142, the one-sided 95% upper limit for the rate is about 2.1% (3 divided by 142).
analysis.preregistration_detail: The six parent trials are registered; this pooled analysis of flashbacks has no registered protocol.
analysis.selective_reporting: All 13 cases are tabulated individually (Table 2), which limits selective reporting.
analysis.power: The authors note that 142 people are too few to assess a rare condition such as HPPD.

interpretation_gap.results_show: About 1 in 11 healthy, screened trial participants who received LSD and/or psilocybin reported some flashback-like experience when asked at the end of the study, mostly a single, brief visual change in the days after the last session, felt as neutral or pleasant. Two (1.4%) found it distressing, one of whom then had panic attacks and left the study; one person had brief, benign visual flashbacks over seven months. No one reported impairment of daily life and no one met criteria for HPPD.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract calls the phenomenon common, occurring in up to 9.2% of healthy subjects, and the paper concludes that flashbacks are not a clinically relevant problem in controlled studies with healthy participants. Gaps: (1) 9.2% is the overall rate, not an upper limit (14.3% among those given both drugs), and without a no-drug comparison the rate cannot be attributed to the drugs, as the Discussion itself acknowledges; (2) ‘not clinically relevant’ sits beside one participant who developed panic attacks after a flashback and dropped out, and another who dropped out after a very difficult session followed by distressing flashbacks; (3) the Discussion says both distressing cases resolved within a week of drug administration, although one began 17 days after psilocybin; (4) the absence of HPPD in 142 people cannot exclude a rate of up to about 2%.

timeline.event: Studerus et al. pooled analysis of psilocybin studies in 110 healthy participants, finding spontaneous altered states in about 10% both before and after dosing (as cited by this paper).
Vizeli and Liechti pooled analysis of MDMA studies in 131 healthy participants from the same group, with flashback-like experiences in 9% (6.5% beyond 24 hours), as cited by this paper.
This pooled analysis of LSD and psilocybin trials.
Evens et al. systematic review of subacute effects of psychedelics, which lists headaches, sleep problems and single distressing events among after-effects in the month after use

replication.where_it_stands: Consistent with earlier pooled analyses of controlled studies (psilocybin; MDMA, from the same group) in which roughly one in ten participants reported flashback-like or spontaneous altered experiences, much lower than the 15 to 75% quoted from naturalistic studies. None of these analyses compares with a no-drug rate, and all concern screened volunteers.

The other authors declare no competing interests.
funding.affiliations_note: The analysis was done by the group that ran all six trials; one funder of the contributing trials is a company that employs the senior trial investigator as a consultant.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study of people taking LSD or psilocybin within and outside research settings, with a standardized flashback and HPPD questionnaire given before dosing (to establish the no-drug rate) and at fixed times for at least a year afterwards to everyone, including people with psychiatric histories or frequent use.

domains.domain: 1. Sample frame appropriate to the target population
domains.note: Appropriate for the paper's stated target, healthy participants of controlled studies; not representative of people who use LSD or psilocybin outside research.

domains.domain: 2. Participants sampled in an appropriate way
domains.note: All participants of all the group's LSD and psilocybin trials up to April 2021.
Enough to describe a frequency near 9%; too small to estimate a rare condition such as HPPD, as the authors note.

domains.domain: 4. Subjects and setting described in detail
domains.note: Trial-by-trial demographics, drug histories and visit intervals in Table 1.

domains.domain: 5. Data analysis with sufficient coverage of the identified sample
domains.note: Whether every participant, including those who left after a session, had an end-of-study visit is not stated.

domains.domain: 6. Valid methods used to identify the condition
domains.note: ICD-10 and DSM-5 definitions applied to answers to open questions; no validated instrument.

domains.domain: 7. Condition measured in a standard, reliable way for all participants
domains.note: The interval from last session to the end-of-study visit ranged from 2 to 193 days; follow-up was offered only to those who reported flashbacks.
Percentages without confidence intervals; the simulation of the chance of observing no HPPD case is appropriate.

domains.domain: 9. Adequate response rate, or low response managed appropriately
domains.note: Coverage of the end-of-study visit is not stated; 12 of 13 responded to follow-up.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: Editors' summary of the JBI checklist: moderate risk of bias for the frequency of reported flashbacks in screened trial volunteers, mainly because the question was asked once at very different intervals, without a standard instrument, and follow-up covered only those who reported flashbacks, which could undercount late or forgotten experiences; the lack of a no-drug comparison could overcount them. The paper may be cited for the frequency and character of flashbacks reported by healthy, screened participants of controlled LSD and psilocybin trials and for the absence of HPPD in 142 such people (with its upper limit); it should not be cited for rates in recreational use or as showing that the drugs cause the reported experiences.

key_findings.finding: 142 healthy participants (146 enrolled; 4 left before any drug) from six double-blind placebo-controlled crossover trials: 90 received LSD only, 24 psilocybin only and 28 both; 74 women; mean age 31.7; previous hallucinogen use in 30.3%.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Studies included in analysis, 2nd paragraph; Results › Subject characteristics, 1st paragraph; Table 1

key_findings.finding: At the end-of-study visit, 13 of 142 (9.2%) reported flashback phenomena: 7 of 90 after LSD only (7.8%), 2 of 24 after psilocybin only (8.3%) and 4 of 28 after both (14.3%); 10 of the 13 were women.
key_findings.locator: Results › Flashback phenomena at end-of-study visit, 1st paragraph

key_findings.finding: Flashbacks were visual in 11 of 13 (with auditory, cognitive or self-disintegration features in 3) and purely emotional in 2; they lasted seconds (69.2%) or minutes (23.1%), hours in one case; 53.8% happened once; in all but two cases they were limited to the week after the last drug administration; more than half occurred while relaxing or around falling asleep or waking.
key_findings.locator: Results › Flashback phenomena at end-of-study visit, 1st paragraph; Table 2

key_findings.finding: Flashbacks were neutral or positive for 10 of 13 and distressing for 2 (1.4% of all 142); one was not documented. No one reported impairment of daily life. One distressing case followed an exceptionally difficult session after which the participant left the study; the other was a single episode during escitalopram pretreatment 17 days after psilocybin, followed by panic attacks, after which the participant left the study.
key_findings.locator: Results › Flashback phenomena at end-of-study visit, 2nd paragraph

key_findings.finding: Two participants had more than five episodes: one about 20 brief visual flashbacks within a short period after dosing, and one about 30 brief, benign visual flashbacks over seven months, which had stopped about ten months before follow-up; at follow-up (mean 31.2 months later; 12 of 13 responding) she was the only one reporting recurrence after the end-of-study visit.
key_findings.locator: Results › Flashback phenomena at end-of-study visit, 1st paragraph; Flashback phenomena at follow-up, 1st and 2nd paragraphs

key_findings.finding: No participant met DSM-5 criteria for HPPD. The simulated chance of seeing no case among 142 people was 24.0% if the true incidence were 1%, 5.7% at 2% and 1.3% at 3%.
key_findings.locator: Results › Hallucinogen-persisting perception disorder, 1st paragraph; Methods › Hallucinogen-persisting perception disorder
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation: zero events in 142 gives a one-sided 95% upper limit of about 2.1% for the rate.

key_findings.finding: Three of the 13 people with flashbacks had also received escitalopram, d-amphetamine or MDMA in the trials; the authors note that rates in naturalistic studies (15 to 75%) are much higher, and that a pooled MDMA analysis by the same group found flashback-like experiences in 9% (6.5% beyond 24 hours).

The authors list as limitations the sample size (especially for HPPD), varying doses and substances, likely positive attitudes and prior drug experience of participants, follow-up only of those who reported flashbacks at different intervals, and exclusion of people with mental disorders.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract gives 25 participants for the psilocybin-and-escitalopram trial, while the Methods and Table 1 give 24; the abstract's four groups add up to 143, not 142.
reporting_issues.consequence: Typographical; the denominators used for the percentages (24 for psilocybin only) follow Table 1.

reporting_issues.issue: The Methods assign the two single-dose LSD trials their sample sizes the other way round from Table 1 (the lower-dose trial has 24 participants in Table 1 and 16 in the text).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the doses and sizes are recorded in the exposure field as in Table 1.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion states that both distressing cases resolved spontaneously within a week of drug administration, but the Results describe one as starting 17 days after psilocybin and being followed by panic attacks.
reporting_issues.consequence: The Discussion understates one distressing case; the Results text should be followed.

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract describes flashbacks as occurring in up to 9.2% of healthy subjects, while 14.3% of those who received both drugs reported them.
reporting_issues.consequence: 9.2% is the overall rate, not an upper limit.
